Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A.Francisco Gold Condominium II, EDSA corner Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City Telephone Number 925.11.48 • 925.88.88 • 925.03.32 www.dilg.gov.ph LEGAL SERVICE DILG Lega Opinion No. 12, S. 2013 RI) BLANDINO MACEDA, CESO 111 DILG Regional Office No. 5 Rizal St., Legaspi City 4500 Dear RI) Maceda, This pertains to your Memorandum dated 19 February 2013 requesting this Department's opinion on the controversy involving the approval of the CY 2013 Provincial Annual Budget and Annual Investment Plan by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan (SP) of Masbate. Your query was impelled by the request of Hon. Julius M. Tuason, SP Member of Masbate, for the Regional Office of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) to withhold its review or approval of the aforementioned measures, claiming the nullity of the same for being passed by the SP of Masbate in a regular session without the benefit of the requisite quorum. Accordingly, Director Rebecca B. Olayon of the DBM Regional Office No. 5 referred the issue to your office for clarification, in view of an opinion earlier rendered by DILG Provincial Director (PD) Renato S. Alaurin. Particularly, the inquiry revolves around the regular session conducted by the SP of Masbate on 10 December 2012. Per your correspondence and its attachments, the SP Of Masbate is composed of fourteen (14) Members, viz.: l. Hon. Vicente Homer B. Revil — Vice-Governor/Presiding Officer 2. Hon. Alfredo L. Alim — SP Member (1st District) 3. Hon. Cherry C. Abapo — SP Member (1st District) 4. Hon. Juan P. Sanchez, Sr. — SP Member (2nd District) 5. Hon. Julius M. Tuason — SP Member (2nd District) 6. Hon. Lovely S. Abapo — SP Member (2nd District) 7. Hon. Enrique O. Legaspi III — SP Member (2nd District) 8. Hon. Hamilcar P. Arregadas II — SP Member (3rd District) 9. Hon. Ricar N. Vasquez - SP Member (3rd District) IO. Hon. Albert Vincent A. Chu - SP Member (3rd District) 11. Hon. John Henry D. Naga - SP Member (3rd District) 12. Hon. Alberto R. Abayon — PCL President, Ex-Officio 13. Hon. Manuel F. Hermosa — Liga President, Ex Officio 14. Hon. Jeralph C. Sanchez — SKPF President, Ex Officio In the questioned 10 December 2012 regular session, only seven (7) of the fourteen (14) SP Members were present, including the vice-governor. SP Members Henry D. Naga and Enrique O. Legaspi III were allegedly both in Manila, and SP Member Jeralph C. Sanchez was allegedly in Cebu. RS more lun in the Phi. '

Page 12 Believing that the three (3) absent SP Members were outside the jurisdiction of the sanggunian to compel their attendance under Section 53 (b) of the Local Government Code (LGC) of 1991, and based on this Department's Legal Opinion No. 9, S. 2005 (or the "Talaran Case" as referred to in your instant query), the present members voted to declare the existence of a quorum, and thereafter conducted the regular session. On IO December 2012, SP Member Julius M. Tuazon wrote DILG PD Renato S. Alaurin inquiring about the validity of the subject session and the applicability of the aforementioned DILG legal opinion. The said inquiry was answered by PD Alaurin on the same date, wherein he opined that the Talaran Case is inapplicable to the session in question by reason of the absence of the circumstances required in the three (3) Supreme Court doctrines laid down in Gamboa vs. Aguirre, Jr. (310 SCRA 867), Paredes vs. Antillon (3 SCRA 662), and Grapilon vs. Municipality of Carigara, Leyte (2 SCRA 103), all of which were cited and dissected in the Talaran Case. Subsequently, SP Member Tuason again wrote PD Alaurin on 17 January 2013, inquiring about the applicability of Zamora vs. Caballero (G.R. No. 147767, 14 January 2004) to the case at bar, and the "seeming different stand of the DILG in DILG Opinion NO. 09 — 2005 (Talaran Case)" in relation to the same case. In a letter dated 18 January 2013, PD Alaurin replied to SP Member Tuason's query, stating, among others, that the Talaran case is not in conflict with the ruling of the Supreme Court in Zamora vs. Caballero, and that "as to the legality of the enactments approved by the SP in that session, the absence of the conditions required by the doctrines in the Talaran Case and the proper determination of the quorum as laid forth in the Zamora vs. Caballero case serve as the bases for their nullity and being void in the first place." Hence, your request for guidance as to whether those SP Members who were outside the province at the time of the questioned session could also be excluded from the determination of quorum. The core of the instant query revolves around the aforementioned letters dated IO December 2012 and 18 January 2013 of PD Alaurin which predominantly held that the Talaran case is not applicable to the session conducted by the SP of Masbate on IO December 2012. At the outset, we have time and again clarified the Department's duty of implementing the Local Government Code via, inter alia, the rendition of legal opinions. Legal opinions are executive constructions given by the government agency concerned on a particular law it is tasked to implement. However, legal opinions have its limitations, considering that the principles laid down in such opinions rendered by this Department are principally based on the facts presented by the requesting party and the attachments included thereto. Moreover, it is to be noted that since the instant issue involves measures which were duly enacted by the SP of Masbate, such approved acts enjoy the presumption of validity, and the SP is likewise presumed to have carried out its function regularly in enacting the said measures, pursuant to Rule 131, Section 3 (m) Of the Rules of Court.

gel 3 Be that as it may, we shall render our opinion on the matter at hand considering the necessity LO elucidate on the effect of the case of Zamora vs. Caballero on a previous opinion rendered by the Department. To begin with, it is our opinion that the ruling in the case of Zamora vs. Caballero may be applied in the instant case. In the said case, a Sangguniang Panlalawigan Member of Campostela Valley challenged the validity of the special session of February 8, 2001 for lack of quorum, there being only seven members of the sanggunian in attendance, with the sanggunian having a total membership of fourteen (14). Respondents, on the other hand, contended that since one Board Member was in the United States at the time the questioned acts were executed and resolutions adopted, the actual number of Board Members then in the country was thirteen (13) which should be the basis of the determination of a quorum. Branch 3 of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Nabunturan, Compostela Valley dismissed the petition, and applied the ruling of the Supreme Court in Avelino vs. Cuenco. The RTC held: "Gemma Theresa M. Sotto should not be counted as member for the purpose of determining the number to constitute a quorum because she is in the United States of America. However, sub-paragraph (b) [of section 53 of the Local Government Code] states and provides for compulsion of any member absent without any justifiable cause. This is interpreted by the Supreme Court in the case of Jose Avelino, petitioner vs. Mariano J. Cuenco, respondent, G.R. No. L-2821, March 4, 1949. Gemma Theresa M. Sotto is beyond the reach of the legal processes of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and could not be arrested to compel her to attend its session. Quorum should be determined on the basis of the actual number of members of the body concerned rather than upon its full membership which is fourteen (14). Therefore, in this case, with seven (7) members of the thirteen (13) members present in constitutive of a quorum. The Supreme Court held that the RTC erred in making such ruling, and instead ruled that the RTC should have based its determination of the existence of a quorum on the total number of members of the Sanggunian without regard to the filing of a leave of absence by Board Member Sotto. The Court ruled, and we quote: "On the applicability of Avelino to the present case: The issue in said case was whether there was a quorum in a meeting attended by only 12 of 24 senators, one having been in the hospital while another was out of the country. This Court held that although the total membership of the Senate was 24, the presence of 12 members already constituted a quorum since the 24th member was outside the country and beyond the coercive power of the Senate. In the instant case, there is nothing on record, save for respondents' allegation, to show that Board Member Sotto was out of the country and to thereby conclude that she was outside the coercive power of the Sanggunian

Page 14 when the February 8 and 26, 2001 sessions were held. In fact it is undisputed that the leave form filed by said Board Member before the Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) did not mention that she was going out of the country. Petitioner's contention that the trial court cannot take judicial notice of Board Member Sotto's whereabouts is thus well taken. On this score, the instant case is outside the application of the doctrine in Avelino. Also, in Avelino, the legislative body involved was the Senate and the applicable rule on quorum was that embodied in Article VI, Section IO of the 1935 Constitution which reads: Section IO. x xx (2) A majority of each House shall constitute a quorum to do business, but a smaller number may adjourn from day to day and may compel the attendance of absent Members in such manner and under such penalties as such House may provide. (Emphasis supplied) The present case, however, involves a local legislative body, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Compostela Valley Province, and the applicable rule respecting quorum is found in Section 53(a) of the LGC which provides: Section 53. Quorum.- (a) A majority of all members of the sanggunian who have been elected and qualified shall constitute a quorum to transact official business. Should a question Of quorum be raised during a session, the presiding officer shall immediately proceed to call the roll of the members and thereafter announce the results. (Emphasis supplied) "Quorum" is defined as that number of members of a body which, when legally assembled in their proper places, will enable the body to transact its proper business or that number which makes a lawful body and gives it power to pass upon a law or ordinance or do any valid act. "Majority," when required to constitute a quorum, means the number greater than half or more than half of any total. In fine, the entire membership must be taken into account in computing the quorum of the sangguniangpanlalawigan, for while the constitution merely states that "majority of each House shall constitute a quorum," Section 53 of the LGC is more exacting as it requires that the "majority of all members of the sanggunian . . . elected and qualified' shall constitute a quorum. The difference in the wordings Of the Constitution and the LGC is not merely "a matter of style and writing" as respondents would argue, but is actually a matter of "meaning and intention." The qualification in the LGC that the majority be based on those "elected and qualified" was meant to allow sanggunians to function even when not all members thereof have been proclaimed. And, while the intent of the legislature in qualifying the quorum requirement was to allow sangguniansto function even when not all members

thereof have been proclaimed and have assumed office, the provision necessarily applies when, after all the members of the sanggunian have assumed office, one or some of its members file for leave. What should be important then is the concurrence of election to and qualification for the office. And election to, and qualification as member of, a local legislative body are not altered by the simple expedient of filing a leave of absence. " Applying the foregoing principles to the instant case, we are inclined to believe that there appears to be legal infirmity in the session conducted by the SP of Masbate on IO December 2012 since the absence of SP Members Henry D. Naga, Enrique O. Legaspi III, and Jeralph C. Sanchez did not alter their election to, and qualification as member of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Masbate, which necessarily does not justify the reduction of number required to constitute a quorum for that particular session. It is to be noted that the Supreme Court in Zamora vs. Caballero held that the filing of a leave of absence by an SP Member does not justify the reduction of the quorum in a specific sanggunian session, which leads to a reasonable conclusion that in the instant case, the absence without official leave of the aforementioned SP Members in the session dated IO December 2012 should likewise not result to such reduction. This opinion, however, is without prejudice to the competence belonging to the DBM in ultimately determining the validity of the questioned measures, since the said office, pursuant to Section 326 of the LGC, has the primary jurisdiction to "review ordinances authorizing the annual or supplemental appropriations of provinces, xxx. " We hope to have enlightened you on the matter. Very truly yours, JESUS B. Dir LS:O Hon. Julius M. Tuason Sangguniang Panlalawigan.Member Masbate Provincial Office Dir. Rebecca B.
